posts.title: A kinder desk posture
posts.excerpt: There is no perfect way to sit. The best posture is the next one: small changes, often.
posts.content:
Set the top of your screen at eye level and let your feet rest flat. Then stop worrying about holding still.

Every half hour, stand, roll your shoulders and take a slow breath. Movement, not position, is what keeps a back and neck comfortable through the day.

posts.title: Running and your knees
posts.excerpt: Sore knees rarely mean you must stop running. Usually they ask for a slower build-up.
posts.content:
Most running knee pain comes from doing a little too much, a little too soon. Keep easy runs truly easy and add distance by no more than about ten percent a week.

Two short strength sessions a week for hips and thighs make a real difference. Ask us to show you three simple ones.

posts.title: Recovering after knee surgery
posts.excerpt: The first six weeks after a knee operation set the pace for the rest. Here is what we focus on.
posts.content:
Early on, we work on getting the knee fully straight, reducing swelling and walking evenly again. Bending comes gradually.

Bring your surgeon's letter to the first session so we can follow their plan. We check in with you every week and adjust the exercises as the knee settles.

posts.title: Gentle neck mobility
posts.excerpt: Three slow movements, a minute each, for a neck that feels stiff after a long day.
posts.content:
Sit tall and turn your head slowly to each side, only as far as is comfortable. Then tilt each ear towards its shoulder, and finally nod gently.

Breathe out as you move. The aim is ease, not stretch: if anything feels sharp or causes tingling, stop and let us know.

posts.title: Sleep and back pain
posts.excerpt: A sore back and poor sleep feed each other. A few small changes can break the circle.
posts.content:
Lying on your side with a pillow between your knees takes strain off the lower back. On your back, a pillow under the knees does the same.

Getting up, roll onto your side first and push up with your arms. A short, gentle walk in the morning often eases the stiffness.

posts.title: Returning to sport
posts.excerpt: Feeling better is not the same as being ready. How we decide when it is time to play again.
posts.content:
Before returning to sport we test strength, balance and the movements your sport asks for, side by side with the uninjured leg or arm.

Then we plan a step-by-step return: training first, then short matches, then full games. Going a little slower now saves weeks later.
